mappings.note: TP = TQ is what makes OT the perpendicular bisector of the chord (LO-3), and the two right triangles that then give TP rest on the contact right angle (LO-2). Both are load-bearing.
OP = 2a from the 30-60-90 triangle, which needs the right angle at the contact (LO-2); halving the 60 degrees first needs OP to bisect it, which comes from the equal tangents (LO-3).
Incircle radius of a right triangle, found from the tangent-segment decomposition of the sides. Equal tangents drive it; the right angle of the TRIANGLE is given, not the contact angle.
Incircle tangent lengths BL, CM, AN from one unknown and equal tangents at each vertex. Pure LO-3.

r = (a + b - c)/2 needs the equal tangent segments along all three sides (LO-3) AND the fact that the two radii at the right-angle vertex form a square with it, which is the contact perpendicularity (LO-2).
Two steps with different theorems: the CHORD and its distance from the centre give the radius (perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord, LO-4), then the tangent right triangle gives PO (LO-2).
PT comes from the contact right triangle (LO-2), then AB is assembled from AP = AE and BQ = BE, equal tangents from A and from B (LO-3). Both theorems are essential.
The tangent segments chain round the quadrilateral to fix BQ (LO-3), and the radius is then read off because OQBP is a square at the right angle B, which needs the contact perpendicularity (LO-2).
Opposite sides of a circumscribing quadrilateral subtend supplementary angles at the centre, proved from the four pairs of congruent tangent triangles. LO-3.
The statement and proof of LO-2 itself - every other point of the tangent lies outside the circle, so the radius to the contact point is the shortest and therefore perpendicular.
x + y = 180 falls out of the two contact right angles in quadrilateral OAPB. The equal tangent lengths never appear, so LO-2 alone.
Given the angle a TANGENT makes with a CHORD, find the angle that chord subtends at the circumference. Two chord/tangent angle relations in a row - LO-4's own case.
Incircle segments AP and BP given plus the area: the sides are assembled from equal tangent lengths and area = r times s. Equal tangents carry the item.
Ends on an angle at the circumference standing on chord AC, after the tangents fix the central angle. The chord/arc angle step is what separates it from a plain LO-2 angle chase.
The tangent right triangle gives the radius (LO-2), then the chord of 16 cm gives its distance from the centre by the perpendicular-bisector property (LO-4). Two distinct results in one item.
OT is the right bisector of PQ because TP = TQ makes triangle TPQ isosceles and OT bisects the apex angle. Equal tangents are the premise of the whole proof.
Angle AOB = 90 degrees between two parallel tangents and a third: the proof pairs equal tangents at A and at B and halves the two straight angles at the centre. LO-3.
A circumscribing parallelogram is a rhombus, from equal tangent segments forcing adjacent sides equal. The named LO-3 consequence.
Perimeter of PNK equals 2PB because KM = KA and MN = BN collapse the third side. Three applications of equal tangents.

The isosceles triangle from PR = PQ (LO-3) sets the base angles, but the answer is the angle subtended by CHORD RS, found using RS parallel to the tangent PQ - a tangent-and-chord angle, which is LO-4.
AB = CD for common tangents to circles of UNEQUAL radii: the tangents meet at an external point P and equal tangent segments to each circle give the result. LO-3.

An arc-and-central-angle chase with a diameter and a point S on the circle, the tangent contributing only its right angle. The chord/arc angle work is the substance, so LO-4. Angles 1 and 2 are labelled only in the figure, so the printed stem cannot be answered.
AD a diameter and DCB a secant: the chase runs through the angle subtended by arc AC. The chord/arc relation distinguishes it from a plain tangent-radius angle sum.
PC + PD from CA = CQ, DQ = DB and PA = PB - three pairs of equal tangents and nothing else.

The incircle of the backyard: AR = AP and the tangent-segment chain give x (LO-3), while part (ii) asks what kind of quadrilateral BQOR is, which is a square only because the radii meet the tangents at right angles (LO-2).
